"Secular differences in the association between caloric intake, macronutrient intake, and physical activity with obesity" - for similar diet and exercise lifestyle, adults heavier in 2008 than in 1988

I came across this reference from an article in The Atlantic. The conclusion - that there must be some unknown factor causing people to get fat - is so bizarro, they are so deeply mired in the "calorie is a calorie" model, that they would rather speculate about extraordinary causes than actually question their paradigm.

Chemical changes in the environment from pesticides and flame retardant - a fairly standard bit of hand waving, that kind of correlation should be relatively easy to find - are farmers getting fatter?

Prescription drug use - might explain some of the numbers for adults, but wouldn't apply to children.

Changes to gut bacteria - by far the most supernatural explanation of the three, and it still fails to explain why there would be such a widespread effect.

But I think if they looked at the actual composition of the food that people were eating, types of fat, types of sugar, you would find hormonal imbalance issues hidden there. And with sugar, the increased prevalence of high fructose corn syrup in so much food, between 1988 and 2008, would seem to be significant.

Doctor Who rumour: feature length specials replacing traditional structure?

I do think 2017 would be a good time for a reboot. New show runner, new Doctor & new companion. That give's Capaldi a nice 3-4 year run. I don't see them shortening the number of episodes anytime soon unless maybe the American ratings decrease.
God yes I completely agree. I think shortening the eps aired with longer runtime would be terrible! I think it would absolutely ruin the momentum of an episode.

Ooh, gosh, I didn't realise that 2017 would have given Capaldi a four year stretch - I suppose it's just because I've not really seen it written down.

I think the reason they'd shorten the number of episodes is to get their house in order, as it were. Moffat needs to have a more human schedule to be able to do Sherlock and Doctor Who, and I think if the number of episodes were to be reduced then it allows him to still have a direct influence in Who, without needing to step down from either show.

It'd probably act as a transitional phase to let a new production team settle in for 2017 - hopefully for another year or so with Capaldi.

Not sure I agree that the current thread should abandoned with a reboot - Personally, I liked all of the Doctors in this run. Each of them brought a new aspect to a single character played at different times during that characters life. I hope this rumor turns out to be false (fewer but feature length episodes) as there are a great number of episodes that played a great story in the single episode format (I really liked "Blink" with David Tenant. Just a great episode that really had little to do with the Doctor. )

You're right that having more episodes lets them play around with the format, definitely. I think it'd be interesting to see what they could do with feature length specials - maybe 4 in a year? - but I wouldn't want a permanent switch to that format.

The occasional 2 or 3 part story (thinking of DT's final story) is good but I am skeptical of a set schedule of 2 hour shows. It makes the time requirement take precedence over the story or character development. I feel that MA/WF episodes started with a good story but then were "padded" to fill 2 episodes - the choices made about the "filler" used didn't seem to advance characters or the story. "Under the lake" is starting out with this weakness of "filler" - my opinion.

If the schedule is kept at single hour format then the story stays the focus and not the time requirement (with the occasional story that justifies 2 or even 3 hours). Take "Day of the Doctor", I think the story would have supported 2 hours (I think John Hurt alone would have justified at least an hour). Some of the Christmas specials could benefit from a longer format but if the schedule dictates the 2 hour format then the "side" stories (I just think "Blink" and "Love and Monsters" were great episodes that gave a glimpse of non-companions whose lives are touched by the Doctor. These "side story" episodes" also allow a lightness showing situations when the Doctor isn't saving the world, just a small piece.

Glad to hear that you're a fan of Love & Monsters - I like it very much, and I'm always sad to hear it dismissed by fans. The series would definitely suffer if it lost those smaller "side pieces", as you called them.

I guess I don't get out enough (or maybe I just haven't had enough discussions with those who have seen lots of episodes). I personally can't see why anyone wouldn't like L&M. It was fun, lighthearted, introduced "Clom" (SP?) - Clom is mentioned (I think) as one of the missing planets in Stolen Earth/Journey's End . I can't "gush" enough about the importance of episodes like L&M. The story was classic - a little boy sees the Doctor when young and lives to adulthood thinking the Doctor is to blame - meets some other people who have let their personal lives be thrown off track by the Doctor's presence - meets a girl - falls for the temptation of an imposter.... (especially liked how the story ended, "we have a love life, of sorts...") What's not to like?

I started doing some looking and can't seem to find more episodes that were a story that was as Doctor-lite as L&M and Blink. Am curious why Moffat doesn't try to put more of these "little" sideline stories into the lineup. ("Flatline" was close as the Doctor spent most of the episode in that tiny Tardis).

They were originally borne because of scheduling requirements, essentially - they needed to reduce the amount of time David Tennant and Billie Piper spent filming, so that their schedule wasn't quite so brutal. They've since decided, basically, to do it in the style of Flatline - if they limit the filming of an actor to one location, they can do it faster. Same principle with The Girl Who Waited. Which is nice, on the one hand, since it means we can see more of the two lead actors, but it's a shame not to be able to have those quieter, more intimate stories.

Glad you liked Love & Monsters - it's much maligned, so it's always nice when someone sticks up for it.
Hadn't heard that before - sure sounds like it's the explanation. Sad though, it suggests that Moffat didn't view these as important episodes. More's the pity....
